question: A school's exams officer has been asked to plan a new revision-support programme for the summer term and intends to use Claude to help build the plan. What should she do first?
options: A) Have three colleagues each request their own plan and compare the four versions later
B) Request the plan and next year's examination timetable in one long single message
C) Ask Claude for a general revision-programme plan and adapt whatever it produces
D) Set out the real constraints — dates, staffing, rooms, budget — then ask for a plan
correct_answers: D) Set out the real constraints — dates, staffing, rooms, budget — then ask for a plan
explanations: Comparing four unconstrained plans multiplies the work without adding information, because none of them was told what has to be true.
Combining two unrelated planning problems in one request makes both weaker and makes it harder to see which answer belongs to which.
A generic plan built on unstated constraints has to be unpicked afterwards, and the assumptions it made stay invisible while she adapts it.

Correct. A plan is only useful if it respects the constraints it has to live inside. Stating dates, staffing, rooms and budget up front is what turns a generic outline into something the school can actually run.
